title: Guest Post: We're having the wrong conversation about legal technology: A call to measure the AI metrics that matter
author: Rob Beard

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s buyer-led transformation thesis and materially extends it with an in-house outcome framework: measure completed operational gains, distinguish them from projected insourcing and automation, and use buyer pressure to connect AI efficiency to outside-counsel dependence and billing reform.
qs: - Reduction in time to contract (target 75%): We have thus far achieved a 78% reduction in contract review time.
- Reduction in outside counsel dependency on volume matters (target 60%): we are on track to reduce outside counsel dependency by 50%+ for volume, repetitive matters.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s customer-outcome orientation and materially develops its implementation and evidence agenda: vendors should demonstrate time, cost and strategic-capacity gains, align incentives with customers, and disclose failures as well as successes. It does not substantively address apprenticeship or verification, and offers recommendations rather than measured results.
qs: To vendors: Show us the time saved, the costs reduced, and the strategic capacity created.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s operating-model and bargaining-shift thesis, then materially develops it with a concrete in-house target for reducing dependence on outside counsel and a buyer-side framework for demanding evidence of client-level efficiency rather than adoption counts.
qs: - Reduction in outside counsel dependency on volume matters (target 60%): we are on track to reduce outside counsel dependency by 50%+ for volume, repetitive matters.

Rather than being content to know the number of licenses/seats our outside counsel have bought, or that they are using AI, we should ask all our partners the same types of questions I'm asking Coherent's legal team:  - How has your use of AI created efficiency gains for our legal team?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI’s value depends on workflow integration and task-level outcomes rather than adoption alone, and materially extends the cluster with buyer-side metrics and a concrete in-house contract-review case. Its broader transformation and billable-hour claims are more predictive, and it gives limited attention to verification or jagged capability.
qs: - Reduction in time to contract (target 75%): We have thus far achieved a 78% reduction in contract review time.

kp.k: Measure customer value rather than vendor adoption
kp.d: Beard argues that the debate over Harvey's user numbers and software utilization privileges vendor and investor success over outcomes for in-house legal teams. He reports that Harvey claimed stronger metrics than previously claimed, without endorsing or verifying those figures. He acknowledges that retention and utilization indicate adoption directionally, but recommends judging AI augmentation by repetitive hours eliminated, resulting cost reductions, reduced outside counsel dependency, and faster, better legal work.
qs: Harvey responded by claiming its metrics were better on these fronts than previously claimed.
Though retention and utilization rates are helpful directionally to understand whether AI is gaining traction, when it comes to the use of AI to augment legal work, what I really want to know is:

How many hours of repetitive tasks did our use of AI eliminate (not hours tracked), and how is that reflected in our costs (the total bill, for outside counsel, and internal people cost that can now be redeployed to higher use, for internal teams)?

kp.k: Law-firm and in-house economic incentives differ
kp.d: Beard asserts that most legal technology is built for law firms, whose hourly revenue incentives differ from corporate legal departments' objectives. His proposed metrics therefore prioritize efficiency, turnaround time and value for the buyer rather than law-firm seat purchases or software feature development.
qs: Today, most legal technology is built for law firms, where more billable hours mean more revenue, and therefore metrics like utilization may be helpful.
In-house teams, by contrast, succeed by gaining efficiency, reducing turnaround time, and creating value. We need metrics that measure these goals.
How has using AI reduced dependency on outside counsel (not how many seat licenses does the law firm have)?

kp.k: Coherent pursues an in-house-focused AI partnership
kp.d: Beard describes Coherent partnering with an unnamed AI provider that exclusively serves in-house teams, rather than purchasing off-the-shelf tools and subsequently integrating them into workflows. He presents this approach as following McKinsey's advice to find partners and as enabling accountability for outside counsel savings and redeployment of internal people costs to higher-value work. His expectation of radical transformation is a belief, distinct from the reported operational results.
qs: I have gone all in on AI—and I believe it will radically transform our legal teams for the better.
we're partnering with an AI provider that builds its products and business model from the ground up, specifically to make in-house legal teams better, faster and smarter.

Because they only work with in-house teams, we can hold them and ourselves accountable to metrics like cost savings from work that previously went to outside counsel and productivity gains that allow us to redeploy people costs to higher-value opportunities.

kp.k: Reported contract review reduction exceeds the stated target
kp.d: In this 1 October 2025 practitioner account, Beard reports a 78% reduction in contract review time against a 75% target labeled reduction in time to contract. He identifies quicker, smarter negotiations as the next objective; the reported achievement specifically concerns review time rather than a demonstrated reduction across the entire contracting process.
qs: Reduction in time to contract (target 75%): We have thus far achieved a 78% reduction in contract review time. Now it's on to quicker, smarter negotiations.

kp.k: Outside counsel reduction remains a prospective outcome
kp.d: Beard states that Coherent is on track to reduce outside counsel dependency by 50%+ for volume, repetitive matters, against a 60% target. This is a progress expectation, not a reported completed reduction, and its scope is repetitive volume work rather than all outside legal services.
qs: Reduction in outside counsel dependency on volume matters (target 60%): we are on track to reduce outside counsel dependency by 50%+ for volume, repetitive matters.

kp.k: Task replacement aims to release internal capacity
kp.d: Against a 30% capacity-creation target, Beard reports that Coherent is on track to use AI to replace 30% of previously manual tasks. He frames this as redeploying resources to higher-use activities and predicts the proportion will increase as the team improves, rather than reporting a completed staffing reduction.
qs: Creation of in-house capacity created (target 30%): we are on track to use AI to replace 30% of the tasks previously done manually, so we can unlock value in our legal teams and redeploy assets to higher-use activities. As we get better, this number will increase.

kp.k: Routine-work automation challenges hourly billing and incumbent models
kp.d: Beard argues that AI productivity gains are making old business models obsolete, using the proposition that eliminating 80% of routine work undermines the billable hour. This is a broader business-model argument, not an additional Coherent performance result. He also asserts that AI-native law firms and platforms serving in-house teams are emerging with success defined by eliminated work, and that buyers increasingly demand transparent outcome metrics.
qs: AI is enabling productivity gains that make old business models obsolete. When technology can eliminate 80% of routine work, the billable hour stops making sense.
AI-native law firms and platforms built for in-house teams are emerging, measuring success in repetitive work eliminated, not work managed our hours billed.
In-house legal teams are demanding transparency, sharing real numbers and calling out metrics theater.

kp.k: Require transparent results, implementation lessons and aligned incentives
kp.d: Beard recommends that CLOs ask partners for specific efficiency gains, time to realization, setbacks, lessons from failure and consequences for their business models. He calls on vendors to disclose time savings, cost reductions, strategic capacity and incentive alignment. His stated goal is responsible augmentation and improved cost structures, especially outside counsel costs, while recognizing that outside counsel remains worth its cost for certain tasks.
qs: How long did it take to realize those gains?
What got worse before it got better? What have you learned through failure?
How does the achievement of massive efficiency affect your business model?

I would love to see a dialogue around the kinds of questions we should be asking to ensure our teams and our partners leverage AI (responsibly, of course) to augment our legal teams and improve our cost structures—specifically when it comes to outside counsel costs, which have increased dramatically (and for certain tasks, are well worth the cost).
To vendors: Show us the time saved, the costs reduced, and the strategic capacity created. Show us how our incentives are aligned with yours. Share the full journey—including the challenges.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Beard reports that Coherent has achieved a 78% reduction in contract review time through its AI initiative.
pts.d: Rob Beard, Coherent's chief legal officer, presents this as an achieved result against a 75% target. The reported result concerns contract review time, whereas the broader target concerns time to contract. Quicker and smarter negotiations are described as the next step, not an achieved outcome.

pts.k: Beard projects reduced reliance on outside counsel and greater in-house capacity by automating repetitive tasks.
pts.d: He says Coherent is on track to reduce outside counsel dependency by more than 50% for volume, repetitive matters, against a 60% target. He also says AI is on track to replace 30% of previously manual tasks, allowing personnel resources to be redeployed to higher-value activities. These are progress projections rather than completed results; the article does not equate task replacement with job cuts or quantify realised monetary savings.

pts.k: Beard predicts substantial improvement in legal teams and argues that AI productivity gains undermine existing billing models.
pts.d: Beard explicitly frames AI as augmentation of legal teams. He predicts radical improvement and argues that eliminating routine work makes the billable hour inappropriate. His reference to eliminating 80% of routine work is a general conditional assertion, not a reported Coherent result.

pts.k: Beard describes an emerging market shift toward AI-native providers, in-house-oriented platforms and customer-value metrics.
pts.d: He claims that AI-native law firms and platforms serving in-house teams are emerging and that buyers increasingly demand transparency about actual outcomes. He contrasts vendor adoption and revenue measures with customer outcomes such as work eliminated, lower costs, faster turnaround and additional strategic capacity. These are presented as current market developments without a quantified market-wide evidence base.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Beard's first-person account of Coherent's implementation and internally tracked performance.
pts.d: Beard offers one achieved percentage and two on-track projections from his own legal department. The article provides no measurement methodology, baseline period, sample size, independent validation or monetary savings figures. Its broader predictions about transformation, billing models and market developments are author assertions rather than findings supported by additional datasets. Beard also invokes McKinsey's advice to seek partners as support for the implementation approach, not as evidence of Coherent's results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The achieved and projected results are reported as of 1 October 2025, with no implementation duration or completion deadline.
pts.d: The contract-review reduction is reported as achieved by publication. Outside counsel reductions and manual-task replacement remain on track, while improved negotiations and further capacity gains are prospective. The Coherent account concerns a partnership with a provider focused exclusively on in-house teams; outside counsel reductions specifically concern volume, repetitive matters. The broader billable-hour claim is conditional on technology eliminating 80% of routine work. Beard acknowledges that outside counsel remains worth its cost for certain tasks.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary beneficiaries are corporate legal departments and their companies; outside counsel and vendors face changes in demand, incentives and accountability.
pts.d: Beard focuses on Coherent and other in-house teams, whose lawyers can spend less time on repetitive work and redeploy capacity toward higher-value activities. General counsel, chief legal officers and CFOs are the intended consumers of outcome-based metrics. Outside counsel may receive less volume work and face pressure to explain how AI efficiencies affect bills and business models. Vendors are asked to demonstrate customer savings and aligned incentives rather than merely seat sales or utilisation. The source does not make an access-to-justice claim.
